visuals.heading: Key Ideas at a Glance

items.text: Starting late is a bigger risk than starting imperfectly.
Every graduate job search in India runs through some mix of four channels.
Keep all three lanes running weekly.
Companies come to you on a fixed calendar.
Naukri, LinkedIn, Indeed, Apna, and the government-run National Career Service list far more roles than any single campus drive, open to every graduate regardless of college.

blocks.heading: It Is Not a Complete Strategy

items.text: What campus placements are genuinely good at
A structured, dated process with a known number of rounds, transparent shortlisting criteria, and companies that have already decided to hire freshers from your type of college.

blocks.heading: Referrals: the Channel Most Freshers Skip

items.text: This is the lane with the best odds and the least use.
Most graduates avoid this channel not because it does not work, but because asking for a referral feels awkward.
Search LinkedIn for alumni from your college, past interns at the company, or extended family and neighbourhood contacts working there.

Instead of applying randomly wherever a listing appears, build one working list before you start, and run it as The 3-Lane Application Split: a small referral-first lane, a portal-application lane, and a direct company-outreach lane, worked in parallel every week rather than one after another.
Lane 1: Referral-first companies
The 8-12 companies where you have any real connection, however distant.
Once you are applying through the right lanes, the next filter is whether your application itself clears the screen - human or automated - in front of it.
If the posting says "Excel" and you wrote "spreadsheet tools," you may not clear the filter.

A small project, a internship writeup, a case note, or a shipped piece of work you can link to or describe in one sentence is worth more than a long list of "responsible for" bullets with nothing to show for them.

blocks.heading: Build a Skill Portfolio Alongside Your Job

items.text: A first job pays the bills; it rarely builds your full career on its own.
The right skill mix for your role and goals
Not every high-income skill fits every person or every role - match the skill to your actual target, not to whatever is trending this month.

blocks.heading: So You Don't Quit Early
blocks.sourceSectionTitle: Realistic application-to-offer math, so you don't quit early

rows: Cold application through a job portal
Roughly 2-8% of applications lead to an interview for a role that is not closely targeted
A single corporate opening can draw over a hundred applications, most filtered by automated screening before a human reads them
Targeted application (skills closely matched, tailored resume)
Meaningfully higher than a generic application, though still well under half
Matching the listed skills and keywords closely improves your odds against automated filters
Referral-backed application
Referred candidates are interviewed and hired at clearly higher rates than candidates sourced through other channels, in large employer datasets
Referrals also tend to move faster once you are in the process
Campus placement shortlist
Varies widely by college tier and company
A known, dated process, but the number of companies visiting depends on your college's placement reputation
Role and skill fit
A role close to the skills you actually want to build compounds faster than a slightly higher starting number in an unrelated role
Manager and learning environment
Who you report to in your first year shapes how much you actually learn more than the company brand does
Growth path and review cycle
A clear review and promotion structure tells you when and how your pay is likely to move next, not just where it starts
Job security and company stability
A slightly lower offer at a stable employer can beat a higher offer at a company with hiring or funding uncertainty
Location and real cost of living
A higher number in an expensive city can leave less spare income than a moderate offer in a cheaper one - compare take-home against realistic costs, not the headline figure

visuals.heading: Mistakes That Stall a First Job Search

items.text: Ask your manager directly what "doing well" looks like in concrete terms, instead of guessing.
Ship one small, complete piece of work early, even if it is minor - visible follow-through builds trust faster than busy-looking effort.
Ask specific questions instead of staying quiet to avoid looking unsure; specific questions read as engagement, not weakness.

blocks.heading: Okay to Switch Your First Job Early

items.text: The role was materially misrepresented at hiring - responsibilities, pay, or work conditions differ from what was promised.
You have a documented pattern of unsafe, unethical, or unpaid-dues issues, not a single bad week.
You have already built visible proof of work in your first months and a clearly better-fit opportunity is real, not hypothetical.
Applying to hundreds of roles with one unchanged resume.
Treating campus placements as the only plan.
Waiting to "feel ready" before reaching out for a referral.
Reading rejection as a verdict on your ability.
Ignoring the National Career Service and other government listings.
